findings.text: The opening paragraph says clearly what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves. A newcomer can answer "what is this and why does it matter" from the first lines.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. ... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The title of Athena's own home page names a different project. A newcomer who skims the heading may think the site is about firstmate, or not know which of the two tools is the product.
findings.source: <title> and h1: "Athena explains how firstmate handles work"

findings.text: The second section is the only place that could show Athena's core promise (a commit traced to the request, the models, the cost and the verdict), and it shows an error. A newcomer meets a broken proof right after the pitch.
findings.source: Check it on a real job: "The records of job 20261029-073603-7kqv could not be read here, so no models, verdict or costs are shown: no reading record for job 20261029-073603-7kqv."

findings.text: The page pitches Athena as a tool for making changes, but the showcase is a read-only study, not a change. Because the job evidence is missing, nothing on the page shows the main feature working.
findings.source: Lede: "turns a short request into a change to a code repository" vs. "A study is Athena's written reading of another software project"

findings.text: There is a link to the next step near the top, and the Next steps section gives concrete actions: the prerequisites, git clone, ./setup.sh and an example `athena ask "add a changelog"`. A newcomer knows what to do next.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and the Next steps section

findings.text: This link is aimed at the repository owner and has no explanation. A newcomer does not know whose proposals these are or whether they should click it.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: Most of the page is a detailed state machine of firstmate's internals. It is thorough and traceable, but it is far more than a newcomer to Athena needs. It also gives no short takeaway on what this study shows about Athena's abilities, beyond the opening claim.
findings.source: Sections "States of a piece of work", "Transitions" (t1–t12), "Counters", "Claims and sources" (c1–c45)

findings.text: Several glossary entries say only that the term is not defined. This is honest, but a newcomer is left with words they still cannot understand.
findings.source: Glossary: "The firstmate source does not define a heartbeat." (similar entries for endpoint, wake, durable record, captain call)

findings.text: The page says plainly that nothing was run and every claim comes from reading files. This helps a careful reader judge how far to trust it.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f1: "no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read."

findings.text: The try-it step does not say whether running it will commit to the user's repository or what it will cost before they press Enter. A cautious newcomer has to read the GitHub README to find out.
findings.source: Next steps: "press Enter to run it on your repository."
